target_output:
The big secret behind Google Earth’s incredible detail is that the sharpest images and 3D buildings **do not actually come from satellites.** 

While satellites provide the zoomed-out, global map, the highly detailed, window-accurate 3D cities you see when you zoom in are created using **airplanes, special cameras, and advanced algorithms.**

Here is a breakdown of how Google achieves this:

### 1. Aerial Photography (Airplanes, not Satellites)
When you zoom in closely on a populated area, the imagery switches from satellite data to aerial photography. Google hires fleets of small airplanes to fly over cities in tightly controlled grid patterns. 
* Because these planes are flying at just a few thousand feet (rather than hundreds of miles up in space like a satellite), the cameras can capture incredibly sharp details.
* The planes are equipped with special camera rigs that take photos not just straight down, but at 45-degree angles in multiple directions (North, South, East, and West). 

### 2. Photogrammetry (How 3D is made)
To create the 3D buildings, Google uses a science called **photogrammetry**. 
* Think about how human vision works: because your two eyes see the world from slightly different angles, your brain can calculate depth. 
* Google does the same thing with computers. Because the airplanes take thousands of overlapping photos of the same building from different angles, Google’s software can calculate the exact height, depth, and shape of that building. 
* The computer generates a blank, 3D geometric shape (a "mesh") of the city based on these calculations.

### 3. "Draping" the Textures
Once the computer has built the blank 3D shape of a building, it needs to be painted. The software takes the actual high-resolution photographs taken by the airplanes and "drapes" or stretches them over the 3D shapes. 
* This is why the number of windows is correct: **nobody modeled the windows by hand.** You are looking at an actual photograph of the building stretched over a 3D block.

### 4. Google Street View
To make the sides of buildings look even sharper, Google’s algorithms often combine the aerial photography from the planes with ground-level photography captured by **Google Street View cars**. The computers stitch the roof data from the planes together with the facade (front) data from the cars, creating a highly realistic 3D model.

### 5. Massive Artificial Intelligence
In the early days of Google Earth, users actually built 3D buildings by hand using a program called SketchUp and submitted them to Google. Today, the process is entirely automated. Google uses massive supercomputers and AI to process petabytes of overlapping photos, calculate the 3D geometry, stitch the images together, remove clouds and shadows, and update the maps automatically.

**Summary:**
When you are zoomed out, you are looking at satellite imagery. But when you zoom into a city and tilt the camera to see the exact number of windows on a 3D building, you are looking at a computer-generated 3D model wrapped in actual photographs taken by low-flying airplanes and Street View cars.

You make a completely fair point! The button in Google Maps and Google Earth is literally labeled **"Satellite,"** which is exactly why almost everyone assumes all the images come from space. 

The short answer is that **Google uses "Satellite" as a simplified catch-all term for the user interface**, even though the imagery is actually a massive patchwork of different technologies. 

Here is why they call it that, and how you can actually prove for yourself that planes are taking the close-up pictures:

### 1. It’s a UI naming convention (for simplicity)
When Google Earth and Google Maps first launched in the early 2000s, the imagery *was* almost entirely from satellites. As technology improved and people wanted to zoom in closer to see their houses, Google started buying aerial (airplane) photography because satellites simply couldn't get sharp enough. 

However, they kept the button named "Satellite" because users were already used to it. Renaming the button to "Satellite / Low-Altitude Airplane / Drone / Street View Blend" would be confusing and clunky. In the tech world, "Satellite view" has just become the generic term for "a photographic map." (Apple Maps and Bing Maps do the exact same thing).

### 2. How to prove it yourself (The Copyright Trick)
You don't have to take my word for it—Google actually tells you exactly where the image is coming from in the app. You just have to look at the tiny text at the very bottom of the screen.

If you open Google Earth or Google Maps on a desktop computer:
* **Zoom all the way out to see the whole globe:** Look at the bottom right corner. The data attribution will say things like **Landsat / Copernicus** or **Maxar Technologies**. These are actual satellite operators.
* **Zoom in closely on a major city (like New York or London):** Watch that tiny text at the bottom. As you zoom in, the satellite companies disappear, and the text will change to names like **Sanborn, Bluesky, Aerometrex, Nearmap**, or local government surveys. These are **aerial surveying companies** that operate fleets of airplanes. 

### 3. The laws of physics
Even the most advanced commercial satellites in the world (like those owned by Maxar, which Google uses) orbit at about 300 to 400 miles above the Earth. Because they have to look through hundreds of miles of moving atmosphere, clouds, and smog, the absolute best resolution they can legally and physically achieve is about **30 centimeters (12 inches) per pixel**. 

At that resolution, a car looks like a recognizable colored blob, but you cannot see crisp window frames, the texture of roof shingles, or the exact shape of a chimney. To get the 3-inch or 1-inch per pixel resolution required for those hyper-realistic 3D cities, a camera *must* be flown inside the atmosphere, usually between 2,000 and 5,000 feet up in a plane.

**In short:** The app calls it "Satellite" because it's a familiar, easy-to-understand button. But the imagery itself is a seamless blend: satellites handle the zoomed-out world, and airplanes handle the zoomed-in cities.

That is a brilliant comparison, and it makes perfect logical sense at first glance! If we can photograph the Moon from 250,000 miles away, 300 miles should be a piece of cake, right?

The reason it doesn't work that way comes down to a mix of **scale, speed, and the laws of physics.** 

Here is why a telescope looking at the Moon is very different from a satellite looking at the Earth:

### 1. The Scale Illusion (Craters are huge)
When you look at a crater on the Moon through a telescope, it looks like a small detail. But that is an optical illusion caused by the massive size of the Moon. 
* The craters you can see with a backyard telescope are **miles across**. 
* Even the **Hubble Space Telescope**, one of the most powerful optical instruments ever built, cannot see anything on the Moon smaller than about **300 feet (90 meters) wide**. It cannot see the Apollo lunar rovers or the flags left behind by astronauts. 
* So, while a telescope can see a 5-mile-wide crater from 250,000 miles away, a satellite trying to photograph a **3-foot-wide window** from 300 miles away requires vastly more zooming power.

### 2. The Speed Problem (17,500 mph)
When you point a telescope at the Moon, the Moon is moving relatively slowly across the sky, allowing the telescope to track it and gather light for a clear, sharp photo.
* Satellites in Low Earth Orbit (where imaging satellites live) are not hovering. To keep from falling out of the sky, they are screaming around the Earth at **17,500 miles per hour** (about 5 miles *per second*).
* Imagine trying to take a crystal-clear, zoomed-in photo of a specific window on a house while driving past it at 17,500 mph. The camera shutter has to be incredibly fast to prevent motion blur, which makes capturing sharp, micro-level details incredibly difficult.

### 3. Looking through the "Soup" (The Atmosphere)
When a telescope looks *up* at the Moon, it is looking through the Earth's atmosphere, but the atmosphere gets thinner very quickly. 
When a satellite looks *down* at the Earth, the light has to bounce off a building and travel back up through the atmosphere. 
* The thickest, dirtiest, most turbulent part of the atmosphere (smog, humidity, heat ripples, clouds) is right at the surface, directly sitting on top of the buildings. 
* Looking down through this is like trying to read a book sitting at the bottom of a deep, rippling swimming pool. The atmosphere bends and distorts the light, which puts a hard physical limit on how sharp a photo from space can be.

### What about Spy Satellites?
You might be wondering: *Doesn't the military have super-advanced spy satellites?* Yes, they do! US military "Keyhole" satellites are essentially the size of the Hubble Space Telescope, but pointed down at Earth. 

However, because of the atmospheric distortion mentioned above, physicists calculate that the absolute maximum resolution even a multi-billion-dollar classified spy satellite can achieve is about **4 inches (10 cm) per pixel**. That is enough to tell if a person is holding a rifle or a shovel, but it still isn't sharp enough to capture the hyper-crisp, multi-angle textures required to build Google's 3D cities. 

Furthermore, Google doesn't have access to classified military satellites. They buy from commercial satellites, which max out around 12 inches (30 cm) per pixel. 

**The Bottom Line:**
To get the 1-inch-per-pixel resolution required to see window frames, roof tiles, and street signs in 3D, you have to bypass the atmosphere and the 17,500 mph speed limit. The only way to do that is to fly an airplane at 3,000 feet, going 150 mph, right over the city.

However, in the scientific and aerospace communities, this is known as a **famous Hollywood myth**. 

It has been repeated in movies (like *Enemy of the State*), TV shows, and even sensationalized documentaries for decades. But when you look at the actual laws of optical physics, reading a newspaper from space is physically impossible with current technology. 

Here is why the "newspaper myth" is busted by physics, and what spy satellites can *actually* see:

### 1. The "Giant Mirror" Problem (The Laws of Physics)
The sharpness of a camera in space is strictly limited by a law of physics called the **diffraction limit**. Simply put, the further away you are, the wider your camera lens (or mirror) must be to capture tiny details. 

* To get a resolution of **4 inches per pixel** from 300 miles away, a satellite needs a mirror that is about **8 feet (2.4 meters) wide**. This is exactly what the US Military's KH-11 spy satellites use (they are basically the Hubble Space Telescope pointed at Earth).
* To read the headline of a **newspaper**, you would need a resolution of about **0.2 inches (0.5 centimeters) per pixel**. 
* To achieve that from 300 miles away, the laws of physics dictate that the satellite would need a mirror roughly **100 to 120 feet wide**. 

We simply do not have rockets big enough to launch a 100-foot solid mirror into space. (For comparison, the James Webb Space Telescope—the most advanced telescope ever built—has a mirror that is only 21 feet wide, and it had to be folded up like origami just to fit in the rocket).

### 2. The 2019 Declassified Spy Photo Proof
For a long time, the exact capabilities of US spy satellites were a closely guarded secret, which allowed rumors like the "newspaper myth" to spread. 

However, in 2019, then-President Donald Trump tweeted a highly classified photo taken by a billion-dollar USA-224 spy satellite of an Iranian rocket launchpad. This caused an uproar in the intelligence community, but it gave civilian scientists a rare chance to see the absolute bleeding-edge of US spy technology.

When optical experts analyzed the photo, they were blown away by how good it was—but they calculated its maximum resolution was roughly **10 centimeters (4 inches) per pixel**. 
* You could clearly see the shape of trucks.
* You could see painted words on the ground (which are huge).
* **But you could not read a license plate, let alone a newspaper.** 

### 3. Google is a Civilian Company
Even if the military *did* possess a secret, physics-defying satellite that could read a newspaper, **Google would not be allowed to use it.**

By law, satellite imagery sold to commercial companies like Google is heavily regulated. Until 2014, the US government legally banned commercial satellites from selling imagery sharper than 50 cm (20 inches) per pixel. Today, that limit has been lowered to about 25 to 30 cm (10 to 12 inches) per pixel. 

### The Verdict
The documentary you watched was unfortunately repeating a very popular urban legend. Spy satellites are incredible machines—they can see a backpack on the ground or tell what kind of fighter jet is parked on a runway. But they cannot read a newspaper, and they cannot capture the crisp, 1-inch-per-pixel, multi-angle 3D textures of window frames and roof shingles you see on Google Earth. 

For that, Google still has to hire pilots to fly airplanes over your city!

It is completely understandable why you would come to that conclusion! If you never see or hear a plane, but you can instantly see a crisp image of your house on your screen, it feels like the only logical explanation is a silent satellite looking down from space. 

However, there are two very common illusions at play here: the illusion that Google Earth is "live," and the illusion of what an aerial survey plane actually sounds like. 

Here is why you’ve never noticed the planes, even though they took the pictures of your house:

### 1. Google Earth is not a live feed (The "Instant" Illusion)
When you zoom in on your house and it instantly becomes crisp, **a camera is not taking a picture of your house at that moment.** 

Google Earth is not a live security camera; it is a giant digital photo album. The image you are looking at was taken months, or often **years**, ago. The reason it gets crisp instantly is simply because your internet connection is quickly downloading a saved image from Google’s servers. 

If you look closely at your driveway on Google Earth, you might notice a car parked there that you haven't owned for years, or a tree that has since been cut down. That is because the photo is old. 

### 2. The planes fly very high (The "Buzzing" Illusion)
When we think of a plane taking photos, we usually imagine a drone hovering over our roof or a low-flying crop duster buzzing loudly over the neighborhood. 

In reality, aerial surveying companies use standard small aircraft (like a Cessna) flying at altitudes between **3,000 and 10,000 feet**. 
* At 5,000 feet, a small airplane doesn't "buzz." If you are inside your house, you won't hear it at all. 
* If you are outside, it just sounds like a faint, distant hum—exactly like the dozens of normal commercial and private planes that fly over your town every single day. They blend perfectly into normal background air traffic.

### 3. They only fly over once every few years
Because it costs a lot of money to hire pilots to map a city, Google does not update the 3D imagery of most neighborhoods very often. For many suburban areas, the 3D map is only updated once every 3 to 5 years. 

When the plane did fly over your house to take that crisp photo, it was likely up there for just a few minutes on a random Tuesday three years ago. You were probably at work, at school, inside watching TV, or simply didn't notice a faint airplane high up in the clouds. 

### 4. Not *every* house is photographed by planes
It is worth noting one exception: if you live in a very rural area, far away from a major city, you might not have 3D buildings on Google Earth. In those rural areas, Google *does* rely purely on satellites, because it’s too expensive to fly planes over empty countryside.
